# Statistics of Association
***



There are several ways to statistically assess the relationship between two variables.
The major differences surround whether the data are cardinal or an ordered/unordered factor.
In all cases, these statistics measure association, not causation.

This chapter asks three questions.

* How strongly are two variables associated?
    * *Pearson correlation*: this is a new statistic for cardinal data, $\hat{r}_{XY}=\hat{c}_{XY}/(\hat{s}_{X}\hat{s}_{Y})$.
    * *Falk's median correlation*: this is a new statistic for cardinal data with outliers.
    * *Kendall's rank correlation and Cramer's V*: these are new statistics for ordered factors and for unordered factors.
* How sure are we?
    * *Bootstrap confidence interval and permutation test*: these assess sampling variability, or the correlation's precision.
      They use the same recipes as [intervals](01_07_Intervals.qmd#resampling-intervals) and [group comparisons](02_12_TwoGroups.qmd#permutation-tests) in earlier chapters.
* Does an association mean that one variable causes the other?
    * *Causation without correlation*: nonlinear or heterogeneous effects can average out, which leaves a correlation near zero.
    * *Correlation without causation*: shared denominators and selection can create a correlation between unrelated variables.

## Cardinal Data

#### **Pearson (Linear) Correlation** {-}

When two variables are cardinal, the foundational measure of how they move together is the covariance.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *covariance* $\hat{c}_{XY}$ is the average product of paired deviations from each variable's mean (where $\hat{m}_{X}$ and $\hat{m}_{Y}$ are the sample means):
$$\hat{c}_{XY} =  \sum_{i=1}^{n} [\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}] [\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}] / n.$$
:::

The *covariance* is useful as a building block for other linear two-variable statistics.
It is positive when $\hat{x}_{i}$ and $\hat{y}_{i}$ tend to be above or below their means together.
It is negative when they tend to move apart, and zero when there is no linear co-movement.
Its units are the units of $\hat{x}_{i}$ times the units of $\hat{y}_{i}$, which makes raw values hard to compare across datasets.
Note that the covariance of $\hat{x}$ with itself is just its variance, $\hat{c}_{XX}=\hat{v}_{X}$, and the standard deviation is $\hat{s}_{X}=\sqrt{\hat{v}_{X}}$.

For an interpretable, unit-free measure that is comparable across datasets, we rescale the covariance.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *Pearson correlation* $\hat{r}_{XY}$ [@Pearson1896] rescales the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations:
$$\hat{r}_{XY} = \frac{ \hat{c}_{XY} }{ \hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y}}.$$
:::

The *Pearson correlation* is useful as the standard unit-free summary of *linear* association.
It is constrained to $[-1, 1]$, with $+1$ for a perfect rising line, $-1$ for a perfect falling line, and $0$ for no linear association.
Because the bounds are the same in every dataset, it lets us compare the strength of two-variable associations across studies.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
What is the correlation for the dataset $\{ (0,0.1) , (1, 0.3), (2, 0.2) \}$?
Find the answer both mathematically and computationally.

Mathematically, there are five steps.

Step 1: Compute the means
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{m}_{X} &= \frac{0+1+2}{3} = 1 \\
\hat{m}_{Y} &= \frac{0.1+0.3+0.2}{3} = 0.2
\end{aligned}$$

Step 2: Compute the deviances
$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\hat{x}_{i}   & 0   & 1 & 2 \\
\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X} & -1  & 0 & 1 \\
\hat{y}_{i}   & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\
\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y}   & -0.1 & 0.1 & 0
\end{array}
$$

Step 3: Compute the Covariance
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{c}_{XY} &=
\sum  (\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})/n
= \left[ (-1)(-0.1) + 0(0.1) + 1(0) \right] \frac{1}{3} 
=  (0.1) \frac{1}{3}
= 1/30
\end{aligned}$$

Step 4: Compute Standard Deviations
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{v}_{X} &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X}\right)^2 / n
= \left[(-1)^2+0^2+1^2 \right]/3
= 2/3 \\
\hat{s}_{X} &= \sqrt{2/3} \\
\hat{v}_{Y} &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y} \right)^2 / n
= \left[ (-0.1)^2+(0.1)^2+0^2 \right]/3
= \left[0.01+0.01\right]/3
= \frac{2}{100} \frac{1}{3} = 2/300 \\
\hat{s}_{Y} &= \sqrt{2/300}
\end{aligned}$$

Step 5: Compute the Correlation
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y}}
&= \frac{1/30}{ \sqrt{2/3}  \sqrt{2/300}}
= \frac{1/30}{ 2 /\sqrt{900}}
= \frac{1/30}{2/30} = 1/2
\end{aligned}$$

Note that this value suggests a positive relationship between the variables.

Computationally, we do the same steps

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create the Data
x0_hat <- c(0, 1, 2)
x0_hat
## [1] 0 1 2
y0_hat <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2)
y0_hat
## [1] 0.1 0.3 0.2

# Compute the Means
m_x_hat <- mean(x0_hat)
m_y_hat <- mean(y0_hat)

# Compute the Deviances
dev_X <- x0_hat - m_x_hat
dev_Y <- y0_hat - m_y_hat

# Compute the Covariance
cov_manual <-  sum(dev_X * dev_Y) / length(x0_hat)

# Compute the Standard Deviations
v_x_hat <- sum(dev_X^2) / length(x0_hat)
s_x_hat <- sqrt(v_x_hat)
v_y_hat <- sum(dev_Y^2) / length(y0_hat)
s_y_hat <- sqrt(v_y_hat)

# Compute the Correlation
cor_manual <- cov_manual / (s_x_hat * s_y_hat)
cor_manual
## [1] 0.5

# Verify with the built-in function
cor(x0_hat, y0_hat)
## [1] 0.5
```
:::

:::

For example, the code below draws a scatterplot of two cardinal variables and computes their covariance and correlation.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Load the Data: 3294 US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage

# Scatterplot
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Workers with more schooling tend to earn more.
# Wages vary a lot at every level of schooling.

# Covariance: cov() divides by n-1 rather than n, which barely matters with n=3294
cov(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
## [1] 1.530776
# The covariance is positive.
# Its units (years times dollars per hour) are hard to judge.

# Correlation
xy_cor <- cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
xy_cor
## [1] 0.2824925
# The correlation of about 0.28 suggests a positive but weak linear association.
```
:::


#### **Hypothesis Testing** {-}

You can conduct hypothesis tests for these statistics using the same procedures we learned for univariate data, [Intervals](01_07_Intervals.qmd).
For example, you can do so by inverting a confidence interval.
The histogram below shows the bootstrap distribution of the correlation, with the interval and $0$ marked.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# xy_hat and xy_cor defined above
# Bootstrap Distribution of Correlation
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
bootstrap_cor <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(bootstrap_cor) ){
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    xy_cor_b <- cor(xy_boot[, 'x_hat'], xy_boot[, 'y_hat'])
    bootstrap_cor[b] <- xy_cor_b
}
hist(bootstrap_cor, breaks=100,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlim=range(c(0, bootstrap_cor)),
    xlab='Correlation',
    main=NA)
title('Bootstrap Distribution', font.main=1)

## Test whether correlation is statistically different from 0
boot_ci <- quantile(bootstrap_cor, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v=boot_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
boot_ci
##      2.5%     97.5% 
## 0.2493675 0.3154663
# The interval, from about 0.25 to 0.32, does not contain 0.
```
:::

:::


Importantly, we can also impose the null hypothesis of no association by reshuffling the data.
If we resample without replacement, this is known as a *permutation test*.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# xy_hat and xy_cor defined above
# Null Permutation Distribution of Correlation
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
null_permutation_cor <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(null_permutation_cor) ){
    xy_perm <- xy_hat
    xy_perm[, 'x_hat'] <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=FALSE), 'x_hat'] ## Reshuffle X
    xy_cor_b <- cor(xy_perm[, 'x_hat'], xy_perm[, 'y_hat'])
    null_permutation_cor[b] <- xy_cor_b
}
hist(null_permutation_cor, breaks=100,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlim=range(c(null_permutation_cor, xy_cor)),
    xlab='Correlation',
    main=NA)
title('Null Permutation Distribution', font.main=1)

## Test whether correlation is statistically different from 0
perm_ci <- quantile(null_permutation_cor, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v=perm_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=xy_cor, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
perm_ci
##        2.5%       97.5% 
## -0.03371363  0.03448983
# The shuffled correlations stay within a few hundredths of 0.
# So the observed correlation of about 0.28 is far outside them.
```
:::

Any association between $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ comes from how their values are paired.
Shuffling $\hat{x}$ keeps its values but breaks the pairing.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}

Is it statistically different from $0$?

:::

So the bootstrap evaluates sampling variability in the world that generated your data.
A permutation test constructs the distribution of the statistic in a world where the null is true.
Altogether, we have

| Distribution| Sample Size per Iteration | Number of Iterations | Mechanism | Typical Purpose |
| -------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |----------------|
Jackknife       | $n-1$ | $n$  | $\hat{x},\hat{y}$: Deterministically leave-one-out observation | Variance estimate (after rescaling) and Normal CI estimate |
Bootstrap       | $n$   | $B$  | $\hat{x},\hat{y}$: Random resample with replacement | Percentile CI estimate |
Null Bootstrap  | $n$   | $B$  | $\hat{x},\hat{y}$: Random resample with replacement and shifted | Percentile CI under imposed null, $p$-values |
Permutation     | $n$   | $B$  | $\hat{x}$: Random resample without replacement | Percentile CI under imposed null of no association, $p$-values |
: Types of resampling

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}

::: {.cell}

    null_bootstrap_cor[b] <- xy_cor_b
}

#### **Robust Correlation** {-}

When the data contain outliers, the mean-based covariance can be misleading and a robust alternative is needed.
The *Falk codeviance* $\tilde{c}_{XY}$ [@Falk1997] replaces the mean-based average in the covariance with the median of paired deviations from each variable's median (where $\tilde{m}_{X}$ and $\tilde{m}_{Y}$ are the sample medians):
$$\tilde{c}_{XY} = \text{Med}\left\{ (\hat{x}_{i} - \tilde{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \tilde{m}_{Y}) \right\}.$$

*Falk's median correlation* $\tilde{r}_{XY}$ rescales the codeviance by the product of the two median absolute deviations:
$$\tilde{r}_{XY} = \frac{ \tilde{c}_{XY} }{ \hat{\text{MAD}}_{X} \hat{\text{MAD}}_{Y}}.$$

The Falk codeviance is useful for cardinal data with outliers or heavy tails, such as income and prices.
One extreme observation can move $\hat{c}_{XY}$ by a lot but $\tilde{c}_{XY}$ by very little.
The median, $\hat{\text{IQR}}$, and $\hat{\text{MAD}}$ from Part 1 are robust for the same reason.^[See [Center/Spread based on Quantiles](01_03_SummaryStatistics.qmd#centerspread-based-on-quantiles). See also the *Theil-Sen Estimator* [@Theil1950; @Sen1968], which may be seen as a precursor.]
Falk's median correlation $\tilde{r}_{XY}$ typically lies in $[-1,1]$ but, unlike the Pearson correlation, not always.
Ties can be a problem, however.
Every observation tied at a median has a product of $0$, so with enough ties the median product is also $0$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
codev <- function(xy) {
  # Compute medians for each column
  med_hat <- apply(xy, 2, median)
  # Subtract the medians from each column
  xm <- sweep(xy, 2, med_hat, '-')
  # Return the median of the paired products
  CoDev <- median(xm[, 1] * xm[, 2])
  return(CoDev)
}
med_cor <- function(xy) {
  # Compute the medians of absolute deviation
  med_hat <- apply(xy, 2, median)
  xm <- sweep(xy, 2, med_hat, '-')
  MadProd <- prod( apply(abs(xm), 2, median) )
  # Return the robust correlation measure
  return( codev(xy) / MadProd)
}
# xy_hat defined above
xy_codev <- codev(xy_hat)
xy_codev
## [1] 0
xy_med_cor <- med_cor(xy_hat)
xy_med_cor
## [1] 0
# Both are exactly 0, although the Pearson correlation is about 0.28.
# The median worker has 12 years of schooling, and so do 36% of all workers.
# Their products are all 0, and the median product falls among them.
```
:::


:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Compute the Codeviance for the dataset $\{(1,2),(2,1),(3,4),(4,3),(5,6)\}$.

The medians are $\tilde{m}_{X}=3$ and $\tilde{m}_{Y}=3$, giving signed deviations and products

\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
\hat{x}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{X} & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\
\hat{y}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{Y} & -1 & -2 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\
(\hat{x}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{Y}) & 2 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 6
\end{array}

The Codeviance is the median of those products: $\tilde{c}_{XY}=\text{Med}\{0,0,2,2,6\}=2$.
The median absolute deviations are $\hat{\text{MAD}}_{X}=\text{Med}\{0,1,1,2,2\}=1$ and $\hat{\text{MAD}}_{Y}=\text{Med}\{0,1,1,2,3\}=1$, so Falk's median correlation is $\tilde{r}_{XY}=2/(1\cdot1)=2$.
Here $\tilde{r}_{XY}$ exceeds $1$: unlike Pearson's correlation, Falk's median correlation is not confined to $[-1,1]$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
xy0_hat <- cbind(x_hat=c(1,2,3,4,5), y_hat=c(2,1,4,3,6))
codev(xy0_hat)
## [1] 2
med_cor(xy0_hat)
## [1] 2
```
:::

:::

You construct sampling distributions and conduct hypothesis tests for Falk's codeviance and median correlation in the same way you do for Pearson's Correlation statistic.

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Shuffling a variable keeps its ties, so with enough ties every shuffled value is $0$.
Add noise to break the ties, then test whether Falk's median correlation is statistically different from $0$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# xy_hat and med_cor defined above
# Many workers tie at the median years of schooling.
# So shuffling them gives a value of 0 every time.
# Years of schooling are recorded as whole numbers.
# Noise of up to half a year keeps each worker within their recorded year.
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
xy_noise_hat <- xy_hat
xy_noise_hat[, 'x_hat'] <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] + runif(n, -.5, .5)
xy_noise_med_cor <- med_cor(xy_noise_hat)
xy_noise_med_cor
## [1] 0.1286916

# Null Permutation Distribution of Falk's Median Correlation
null_permutation_med_cor <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(null_permutation_med_cor) ){
    xy_perm <- xy_noise_hat
    xy_perm[, 'x_hat'] <- xy_noise_hat[sample(n, replace=FALSE), 'x_hat'] ## Reshuffle X
    xy_med_cor_b <- med_cor(xy_perm)
    null_permutation_med_cor[b] <- xy_med_cor_b
}
hist(null_permutation_med_cor, breaks=100,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlim=range(c(null_permutation_med_cor, xy_noise_med_cor)),
    xlab="Falk's Median Correlation",
    main=NA)
title('Null Permutation Distribution', font.main=1)

## Test whether Falk's median correlation is statistically different from 0
abline(v=quantile(null_permutation_med_cor, probs=c(0.025, 0.975)), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=xy_noise_med_cor, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
```

## Factor Data

#### **Two Ordered Factors** {-}

When the data are ordered (rankings or ordered categories), we can summarize association by counting which pairs of observations agree in direction.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
*Kendall's rank correlation* $\hat{\text{KT}}$ [@Kendall1938] is the share of variable-pairs that agree in direction (concordant) minus the share that disagree (discordant):
$$\hat{\text{KT}} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i} \sum_{j > i} \text{sgn} \Bigl( (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{x}_{j})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{j}) \Bigr),$$
where the sign function is
$$\text{sgn}(z) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } z > 0\\ 0  & \text{if } z = 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } z < 0 \end{cases}.$$
:::

Kendall's $\hat{\text{KT}}$ is useful for any *monotone* relationship: the values do not have to fall on a straight line, only have consistent ordering.
Because it only uses signs, it works for any ordinal data (rankings, ordered categories) where arithmetic averages are not meaningful.
The bounds $[-1, 1]$ make it directly comparable to the Pearson correlation: a value closer to $+1$ suggests positive association in rankings, $-1$ negative, and $0$ no association in the ordering.
For example, the table below cross-classifies two ordered variables, and $\hat{\text{KT}}$ summarizes it.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Load the Data
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# Group hourly wages into four ordered brackets
wage_bracket <- cut(Wages1[, 'wage'], breaks=c(0, 4, 6, 8, Inf), ordered_result=TRUE)
xy_ord_hat <- data.frame(x_hat=Wages1[, 'school'], y_hat=wage_bracket) # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=wage bracket
table(xy_ord_hat)
##      y_hat
## x_hat (0,4] (4,6] (6,8] (8,Inf]
##    3      0     1     0       0
##    4      1     0     0       1
##    5      2     2     1       0
##    6      4     7     3       0
##    7     11     9     3       1
##    8     51    22     9       4
##    9     90    52    13       6
##    10   169   119    78      33
##    11   214   218   129     100
##    12   365   375   251     197
##    13    63    93    93      90
##    14    50    55    59     100
##    15    13    23    40      58
##    16     0     6     2       8
# Both are ordered categories: 12 years is more than 10.
# The top bracket pays more than the bottom one.

# Kendall's rank correlation uses only the order of the categories
KT <- cor(xy_ord_hat[, 'x_hat'], as.integer(xy_ord_hat[, 'y_hat']), method='kendall')
round(KT, 3)
## [1] 0.236
# The value is positive.
# So workers with more schooling tend to be in higher wage brackets.
```
:::


:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Kendall's $\hat{\text{KT}}$ also applies to cardinal data, because it only uses the ordering of the values.
Converting each variable to ranks first does not change the statistic.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# xy_hat defined above
# Convert each variable to ranks
xy_rank_hat <- xy_hat
xy_rank_hat[, 'x_hat'] <- rank(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
xy_rank_hat[, 'y_hat'] <- rank(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
# plot(xy_rank_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1))
KT_rank <- cor(xy_rank_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_rank_hat[, 'y_hat'], method = 'kendall')
round(KT_rank, 3)
## [1] 0.219
# Same value using the raw data
round(cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], method='kendall'), 3)
## [1] 0.219
```
:::

:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Compute Kendall's $\hat{\text{KT}}$ for the dataset $\{(1,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,4)\}$.

With $n=4$ there are $n(n-1)/2=6$ pairs.
For each pair we take the sign of $(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{x}_{j})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{y}_{j})$: a pair is *concordant* ($+1$) if both variables move the same way, *discordant* ($-1$) if they move oppositely.

| Pair | $\hat{x}$ moves | $\hat{y}$ moves | sign |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| (1,1),(2,3) | up | up   | $+1$ |
| (1,1),(3,2) | up | up   | $+1$ |
| (1,1),(4,4) | up | up   | $+1$ |
| (2,3),(3,2) | up | down | $-1$ |
| (2,3),(4,4) | up | up   | $+1$ |
| (3,2),(4,4) | up | up   | $+1$ |
: Concordant and Discordant Pairs

There are $5$ concordant and $1$ discordant pair, so
$$
\hat{\text{KT}} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}\text{sgn}(\cdots) = \frac{2}{4\cdot3}(5-1) = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67.
$$

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cor(c(1,2,3,4), c(1,3,2,4), method='kendall')
## [1] 0.6666667
```
:::

:::

You construct sampling distributions and conduct hypothesis tests for Kendall's rank correlation statistic in the same way you do for Pearson's Correlation statistic and Falk's Codeviance statistic.

#### **Two Unordered Factors** {-}

When neither variable has a meaningful order, we organize the data as a contingency table and summarize the strength of association with a single bounded score.
*Cramer's V* $\hat{\text{CramV}}$ [@Cramer1946] rescales the *chi-squared statistic* $\hat{\chi}^{2}$ into a $[0, 1]$ score for the strength of association between two categorical variables in a $K\times J$ contingency table:
$$\hat{\chi}^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(\hat{o}_{kj} - \hat{e}_{kj})^2}{\hat{e}_{kj}}, \qquad \hat{\text{CramV}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\chi}^2 / n}{\min(J - 1, \, K - 1)}},$$
where $\hat{o}_{kj}$ is the observed frequency in cell $(k, j)$, $\hat{e}_{kj} = \hat{\text{RF}}_{k} \cdot \hat{\text{CF}}_{j} / n$ is the expected frequency under independence, and $\hat{\text{RF}}_{k}=\sum_{j} \hat{o}_{kj}$, $\hat{\text{CF}}_{j}=\sum_{k} \hat{o}_{kj}$ are the row and column totals.

Cramer's V is useful for two unordered categorical variables, such as occupation and region.
Reordering the rows or columns of the table does not change it.
The chi-squared piece measures how far observed counts are from what we would expect if $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ were independent.
Dividing by $n \cdot \min(J - 1, K - 1)$ rescales it into a bounded score, so different tables are comparable.
A value of $0$ suggests no association, and a value closer to $1$ suggests a strong association.

For example, the table below cross-classifies two categorical variables, and the function below computes their Cramer's V.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Pair each worker's sex with a schooling group, as in Comparing Multiple Groups
# The schooling groups have an order, but Cramer's V ignores it.
# So we treat both variables as unordered.
school_g <- cut(Wages1[, 'school'], breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 16), labels=c('<12', '12', '>12'))
xy_cat_hat <- data.frame(x_hat=Wages1[, 'sex'], y_hat=school_g) # x_hat=sex, y_hat=schooling group
table(xy_cat_hat)
##         y_hat
## x_hat    <12  12 >12
##   female 567 594 408
##   male   786 594 345
# Men are more likely than women to have fewer than 12 years of schooling.

CV <- function(xy){
    # Create a contingency table from the categorical variables
    tbl <- table(xy)
    # Compute the chi-square statistic (without Yates' continuity correction)
    chi2 <- chisq.test(tbl, correct=FALSE)[['statistic']]
    # Total sample size
    n <- sum(tbl)
    # Compute the minimum degrees of freedom (min(rows-1, columns-1))
    df_min <- min(nrow(tbl) - 1, ncol(tbl) - 1)
    # Calculate Cramer's V
    V <- sqrt((chi2 / n) / df_min)
    return(V)
}
CV(xy_cat_hat)
## X-squared 
## 0.1007045
# Cramer's V of about 0.10 suggests a weak association.

# DescTools::CramerV( table(xy_cat_hat) )
```
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Compute Cramer's V for this $2\times2$ table of $100$ workers, cross-classifying a college degree against employment.

\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
 & \text{employed} & \text{unemployed} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{degree}    & 30 & 10 & 40\\
\text{no degree} & 20 & 40 & 60\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 50 & 50 & 100
\end{array}

If degree and employment were independent, the expected count in each cell is $\hat{e}_{kj}=\hat{\text{RF}}_{k}\hat{\text{CF}}_{j}/n$.
For the top-left cell, $\hat{e}_{11}=40\cdot50/100=20$; all four expected counts are $(20,20,30,30)$.
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{\chi}^2 &= \frac{(30-20)^2}{20}+\frac{(10-20)^2}{20}+\frac{(20-30)^2}{30}+\frac{(40-30)^2}{30} = 5+5+\frac{10}{3}+\frac{10}{3} = \frac{50}{3} \approx 16.67.
\end{aligned}$$
With $K=2$ rows and $J=2$ columns, $\min(J-1,K-1)=1$, so
$$
\hat{\text{CramV}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\chi}^2/n}{\min(J-1,K-1)}} = \sqrt{\frac{(50/3)/100}{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{6}} \approx 0.41.
$$

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Observed 2x2 table
O <- rbind(degree    = c(employed=30, unemployed=10),
           no_degree = c(20, 40))
n0 <- sum(O)

# Expected counts under independence
E <- outer(rowSums(O), colSums(O)) / n0

# Chi-square statistic and Cramer's V
chi2 <- sum((O - E)^2 / E)
df_min <- min(nrow(O)-1, ncol(O)-1)
c(chi2=chi2, CramerV=sqrt((chi2/n0)/df_min))
##       chi2    CramerV 
## 16.6666667  0.4082483
```
:::

:::

You construct sampling distributions and conduct hypothesis tests for Cramer's V statistic in the same way you do for the other statistics.

## Association is not Causation

None of the tools in this chapter alone identifies what would happen to $Y_{i}$ if we intervened and changed $X_{i}$ [@Holland1986].
Sampling variability is one problem: relationships in the population may not appear in a sample, and apparent sample relationships may not exist in the population.
[Hypothesis tests](#hypothesis-testing) help quantify that uncertainty, but statistical significance does not distinguish association from causation.
Two other problems remain: real relationships can average out, and random data can acquire mechanically induced relationships.
To make both problems concrete, we focus on the Pearson correlation from [Cardinal Data](#cardinal-data) and examine

* Causation without correlation
* Correlation without causation


#### **Causation without correlation** {-}

Examples of the first problem include *nonlinear effects* and *heterogeneous effects* that average out.
For example, wages tend to rise with age early in a career and then flatten or fall, and a minimum wage increase can raise pay for some workers while others lose their jobs.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
n <- 10000

# X causes Y via Y = X^2 + noise
x_sim <- runif(n, min = -1, max = 1)
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.1)
y_sim <- x_sim^2 + epsilon  # clear causal effect of X on Y
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')

# Correlation over the entire range
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Heterogeneous Effects
x_sim <- rnorm(n) # Randomized 'treatment'

# Heterogeneous effects based on group
group <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_sim <- ifelse(group == 1,
            x_sim + epsilon,   # positive effect
            -x_sim + epsilon)  # negative effect
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')

# Correlation in the pooled sample
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



#### **Correlation without causation** {-}
Examples of the second problem include *shared denominators* and *selection bias* that induce correlations.

Consider three completely random variables.
We can induce a mechanical relationship between the first two variables by dividing them both by the third variable.
Per-capita statistics are a common real case, such as crimes per resident and police officers per resident across cities, which share population as the denominator.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## MAIN EXAMPLE
n <- 20000

# Independent components
A <- runif(n)
B <- runif(n)
C <- runif(n)
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(A, B, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='A', ylab='B')
cor_ab <- round(cor(A, B), 2)
title(paste0('Independent Variables\nCor: ', cor_ab), font.main=1)

# Ratios with a shared denominator
x_sim <- A / C
y_sim <- B / C
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('With Common Divisor\nCor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}

# Correlation
cor(x_sim, y_sim)
## [1] 0.8094966
```
:::


Consider an admissions rule into university: applicants are accepted if they have either high test scores or strong extracurriculars.
Even if there is no general relationship between test scores and extracurriculars, you will see one amongst university students.
Real datasets are often selected in a similar way, so their relationships describe the selected group rather than everyone.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

# Independent traits in the population
test_score        <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
extracurriculars  <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Selection above thresholds
threshold <- 1.0
admitted <- (test_score > threshold) | (extracurriculars > threshold)
mean(admitted)  # admission rate
## [1] 0.294

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
# Full population
plot(test_score, extracurriculars,
     pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
     main=NA, xlab='Test Score', ylab='Extracurriculars')
cor_all <- round(cor(test_score, extracurriculars), 2)
title(paste0('General Sample\nCor: ', cor_all), font.main=1)
# Admitted only
plot(test_score[admitted], extracurriculars[admitted],
     pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
     main=NA, xlab='Test Score', ylab='Extracurriculars')
cor_adm <- round(cor(test_score[admitted], extracurriculars[admitted]), 2)
title(paste0('University Sample\nCor: ', cor_adm), font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_14_Associations_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}

## [1] -0.5570494
```

Two variables can also move together because both respond to common factors.

#### **Recall** {-}

The right statistic of association depends on the type of data.
For cardinal data, we computed the Pearson correlation by hand for $\{(0, 0.1), (1, 0.3), (2, 0.2)\}$ and found $\hat{r}_{XY}=1/2$.
For cardinal data with outliers, the Falk codeviance $\tilde{c}_{XY}$ is a robust alternative.
For ordered factors, the six pairs of $\{(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 4)\}$ gave Kendall's $\hat{\text{KT}}=2/3$.
For unordered factors, the $2\times 2$ table of degree and employment gave Cramer's V $\hat{\text{CramV}}=\sqrt{1/6}\approx 0.41$.
These statistics describe association rather than causation.
